p: Each definition is taken from the first sentence of your teacher’s model answers and lesson slides.

head: Term
Definition
rows: Socialisation
The process by which humans learn and internalise their culture’s norms and values.
Culture
The learned and socially constructed way of life of a group, including norms, values, beliefs and traditions.
Norms
Social rules and expectations about how people should behave.
Values
Shared ideas about what a group considers important, desirable or morally right.
Beliefs
Ideas people accept as true about the world.
Tradition
A custom, belief or practice passed between generations.
Material culture
Physical objects associated with a group’s way of life.
Non-material culture
Ideas and meanings, including language, beliefs, values and norms.
Subculture
A recognisable group within a wider culture whose members share distinctive norms, values, interests or styles.
Agents of socialisation
People, groups and institutions through which individuals learn culture, norms and values.
Primary socialisation
The first stage of learning culture, usually through parents or carers.
Secondary socialisation
The continuing process of learning norms, values and roles beyond the earliest learning in the family.
Peer group
People of a similar age or social position who interact and influence one another.
Role model
Someone whose behaviour others observe and may imitate.
Status
A person’s social position or standing.
Sanctions
Rewards or punishments used to encourage conformity to norms.
Social control
The ways groups encourage conformity to norms and discourage unacceptable behaviour.
Nurture
The influence of upbringing, socialisation and environment on development.

p: Socialisation is the process through which humans learn and internalise their culture’s norms and values, which is passed from generation to generation (Giddens, 2006). It begins from the moment of birth and extends to the point of death.

head: Kind
What it means
Example
rows: Primary
The child learns from their family in the home, and learns the expectations the parents have for them. It is the first stage of a life-long process.
A parent teaching a child to say please
Secondary
The child learns what wider society expects of its members, and this generally takes place outside the home.
Education, peer groups, the media, religion
Formal
The process where people are deliberately and consciously taught to follow certain rules.
A teacher teaching the rules of the classroom
Informal
People learn to fit into their culture by watching and learning from others around them. It is unintentional and less obvious.
Copying the way a parent talks

p: Adult socialisation is Parsons’ third stage, tertiary socialisation. It takes place when people need to adapt to new situations such as becoming a parent, changing jobs, or coping with illness or death.
Some textbooks call the workplace a secondary agent; your course treats adult socialisation as a third stage, tertiary socialisation.

list: Through formal processes: deliberate, you must learn these rules, they are consciously taught.
Through informal processes: unintentional, less obvious, perhaps through casual observation of others.
Through agents of socialisation: primary and secondary agents.
Through manipulation: sanctions, expectations, verbal appellations, canalisation.
Through observation of others: imitation, role models, copycat behaviour, differentiated activities.

head: Agent
Facts from your lessons
rows: Family (primary)

Parents are our ‘significant others’. Children learn by imitation, copying the way parents talk or their table manners. Parents can also learn from their children: pester power is children pressuring parents into buying products advertised in the media.
Education (secondary)

Taught in two ways: the formal curriculum (the official or national curriculum) and the hidden curriculum (the social norms children learn without being officially taught, such as punctuality and respect for authority).
Peer group (secondary)

People who are the same age and status as oneself. Groups often form around things in common, and each group has norms and values, so members are encouraged to conform through peer pressure: rewards and sanctions.
Media (secondary)
The media has an impact on the development of gender roles, ethnic identities and social class identities.
Religion (secondary)
Religion can have a profound effect on socialisation. It passes on a parent’s faith and shares religious traditions and rites of passage. The UK has become more secularised.
Workplace (tertiary)
An important agent of adult socialisation and part of our social identity. Learning can be formal, such as training, or informal, such as canteen culture.

p: Social control is the different processes through which society enforces conformity to the norms.
Sanctions are social reactions to either conformity (positive sanctions) or violation (negative sanctions) of the norms.

head: Positive (a reward)
Negative (a punishment)
rows: Formal: given by an organisation with written rules, such as a school, an employer or a court
Graduation ceremony; a merit or certificate at school; promotion at work
Prison sentence; detention; a court fine
Informal: given by anyone in everyday life
A pat on the back; being told ‘Well done’
Time-out at home; being left out of a group; ‘I’m very disappointed in you’

head: Perspective
What it says about socialisation
rows: Functionalist
A consensus view: socialisation unites society in a set of shared norms and values.
Marxist
A conflict view: socialisation gives people the ideas that the powerful promote, and prepares the masses for exploitation.
Feminist
Socialisation prepares us for different gender roles and to accept patriarchy; gender differences are due to culture, not biology.
Interactionist
People interpret meanings, and everyday reactions from others shape their identity.
Postmodernist
People can combine many cultural influences when they build an identity.

head: Writer
What to say
rows: Parsons
Three stages: primary, secondary and tertiary socialisation. All societies have functional prerequisites, and a shared culture provides for these needs.
Giddens (2006)
Socialisation is the process through which humans learn and internalise their culture’s norms and values.
Oakley (1974)
Verbal appellations are labels in the family that teach gender roles. Socialisation perpetuates gender inequality.
Thorne (1993)
School systems also reinforce gender differences.
Bandura
Name linked with imitation: copying what others do.
Sewell
Uses the term ‘cultural comfort zones’: peer groups tend to include people from similar social backgrounds.
Skelton and Francis
Boys tend to dominate the playground space by playing football, whereas girls are pushed to the periphery.
Opie
Children have a street culture from which adults are excluded.
Handel (Interactionist)
In the peer group a child learns to function more independently and to earn a place among people of the same generation.
McRobbie (1970s)
Girls’ magazines tended to encourage romance and ‘keeping a man’, often through domesticity.
Currie (1999)
A dramatic increase in the emphasis on beautification: the concept of ‘slimblondeness’.
Rutherford (2000 onwards)
Growth of men’s magazines such as FHM and Loaded, with a focus on body image.
In 1964, 26% did not identify with any religion. By 2006 this rose to 69%.

p: A five-mark question is marked for AO1 knowledge and understanding (3 marks) and AO2 application (2 marks). A named theory is not an automatic requirement for full marks.
list: D, Define the term: an accurate definition, in the words the course uses.
I, Item link: use specific words from the item and say how they show the term.
E, Explain with an example: a relevant example, with a sentence that explains it.
T, Theory link: a brief, relevant link to a perspective, such as Functionalists or Feminists.

p: A ten-mark ‘using the item, explain’ answer is two PEEL paragraphs, one for each point.
list: P, Point: answer the question in one sentence.
E, Evidence: name a writer, a perspective or a key term that fits your point.
A, Apply the item: quote the item’s own words and say what they show.
E, Explain: join your ideas with because, this means and so.
L, Link back: finish by returning to the wording of the question.
